How do you feel about the amount of superhero movies being released?

Personally, I'm getting a little tired of it. There are way too many and they seem to be finding a formula which is getting very tiring - a few of them do not seem original at all. My opinion, anyway.

They contribute to the an overarching cultural pastiche which is becoming more and more apparent to many. Part of the problem is also that we really haven't developed any new mediums for story telling in the past century or so.

Edit: it's sort of like innovation in the absence of invention. They steal elements from other mediums and use it to great effect. A great example is in the directors cut of The Warriors movie (1979). The movie itself is based on a comic and the comic is based on an ancient Greek tale/myth/story. This is the first example I found where specific elements of the comic book medium were included in the film. Specifically, the directors cut introduces 1-3 second transition scenes in a comic book "style" (page turns, comic frame slides, etc). I have no examples of this for recent comic book adaptations to film, but I'm sure I've seen a few. You would never see these transition styles develop in the film medium naturally, as they are only intuitive for a medium like graphic novels. As a result of this seemingly innovative adaptation it became a cult classic for many.

Most people, myself included, take no issue with this sort of "innovation" or "pastiche" or "mashup". It's simply inevitable. People actually seem to prefer the relatively simple plots which are written time and time again. Pick a piece of classic English literature (Great Expectations) and pick a recent movie (Jupiter ascending), bam, they're the same story about ascending from the working class. Ones a space epic and ones an industrial age England epic, but they're similar. The comic book movies today can blatantly be the same exact story and get away with it because people really don't mind.

Well, if I am only watching these superhero movies from the library, streaming them online for free, or watching a ripped version of it on DVD-RW, then I feel great. I don't have to pay a god damn thing for a movie I know will come out on DVD / Blu-Ray at the library within 3 months after its release on said DVD/BR. ^.^

I mostly feel well reach a point in which the market becomes so over saturated that we reach a heavens gate moment for the genre: a film so bad it effectively kills the genre. I certainly hope not but it could happen...

Heaven's Gate while it was a notorious flop wasn't actually that bad movie. Some critics have even called it a masterpiece. Although, personally, I wouldn't go that far. It's notorious not because it marked the end of a genre - after all there have been loads of westerns since then - but because it marked an end to the era of studios taking risks with Hollywood auteurs directors. Or at least put a major damper on their influence. With it acting as a historical mile stone to that effect.

While you can bemoan that nowadays Hollywood is an extremely cynical corporate based business where no one is interested in taking a risks and only ever interested in bankable commodities. The problem is that when they do take risks or decide to experiment and give creators control of the product it normally doesn't work out for them. And you just end up getting flops like Heaven's Gate. Or more recently movies like John Carter or Hugo.

From a purely business perspective Superhero movies are great because they're normally based on established franchises with in built fans, you can drive them into the ground with sequels and remakes, and even if you screw up you can just retcon your mistakes out.

So far the genre is in the greatest shape imaginable but eventually well have a movie that will scare away investors from the genre.

Meh, This situation only came about because Australia has data caps to begin with, that is you have a quota of the amount of data that you're able to download and if you go over it they slow down your internet, until your plan turns over or you buy more data. I don't think that many other countries have to put up with this absolute bullshit. The perversity of this situation is that it actually encourages you to download more since if you don't use up you allocated quota it's like you're giving them money. That and Australia is always treated like a doormat by corporations. We're only just now getting Netflix for example. There's a reason why piracy is so high in this country.

What the article does not address is where is Netflix making its data availble from? Is it serving it up from data centres in Australia or CDNs (such as Akamai) with nodes available within ISP networks? Or is it expecting local ISPs to pay for the international transit costs? I'm not saying they are not, but it would add more weight to their argument if they are investing in Australia and at least providing local peering.

A large part of the variable cost of global Internet usage for Australia is that we have a relatively low population and sit at the far end of a low bandwith submarine cable network, with no one to help offset costs over the same route except New Zealand. Backhaul is still a significant cost component, and contention ratios have been one of differentiators between local ISPs.
